More than a year ago, House Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy was caught on a hot microphone suggesting that two people in Washington were being paid by Russia: Donald Trump and California Republican Rep. Dana Rohrabacher. McCarthy later apologized and said he was not being serious. Both men were still in office.

A report by The New York Times, however, described a long-running relationship between Rohrabacher and Russian officials, while stopping short of concluding that he was a Russian agent. According to the report, the FBI warned Rohrabacher in 2012 that Russian intelligence officers viewed him as a potential source and had assigned him a code name. The briefing occurred several years before Rohrabacher served as chairman of a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee focused partly on European and Eurasian affairs.

Rohrabacher did not appear to have a formal role in the 2016 Trump campaign, but his contacts with Russian officials and other figures drew political and investigative attention. The FBI and Senate Intelligence Committee were seeking to interview him about an August meeting with Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, Rohrabacher said. Special Counsel Robert S. Mueller III was also reportedly interested in a meeting Rohrabacher had held the previous year with Michael T. Flynn, who later briefly served as President Trump’s national security adviser.

Rohrabacher’s relationship with Russia went back decades. As a young conservative who worked in the Reagan administration, he welcomed the collapse of the Soviet Union and later developed a relationship with Vladimir Putin. In the 1990s, Rohrabacher said, he lost an arm-wrestling match to Putin, who was then a rising Russian political figure.

Rohrabacher denied that he was a Russian asset or that he had knowingly worked for Russian intelligence. He said he did not remember being told that Russian officials regarded him as a source. Former intelligence officials said the FBI and senior members of the House Intelligence Committee had warned him in the Capitol in 2012 that Russian spies were trying to recruit him. Rohrabacher recalled being told that he had been targeted for recruitment, but dismissed the suggestion that he had been acting improperly.

His contacts nonetheless attracted scrutiny. In 2016, he carried a memo concerning Democratic donors from a meeting involving Russian-linked individuals and delivered it to people connected with the Republican Party, according to the Times report. He also met with Assange and with Russian businessmen, including individuals who had faced allegations of criminal conduct. Those contacts, by themselves, did not establish that Rohrabacher was working as a Russian agent.

Rohrabacher said his objective was to improve relations with Moscow and enlist Russian cooperation in combating terrorism. Critics argued that his approach was too accommodating toward the Russian government and its allies, including Syrian President Bashar al-Assad.

Republicans sought to create some distance from Rohrabacher as scrutiny of Russia’s activities in the 2016 election intensified. His influence on the House Foreign Affairs Committee was limited, and he did not retain the subcommittee chairmanship in the next Congress.

Politically, the controversy posed a challenge for Rohrabacher. He was facing a competitive race in California, and opponents cited his positions on Russia and his meetings with Russian-linked figures.

Hans Keirstead, a stem-cell researcher and one of several Democrats seeking the party’s nomination to challenge Rohrabacher, criticized the congressman’s record on Russia and questioned whether his priorities aligned with those of his constituents. Rohrabacher rejected the criticism as a political attack and used the controversy in fundraising appeals.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and other Republican officials criticized a White House request for roughly $44 billion in additional disaster aid, saying it did not appear to meet the needs created by Hurricane Harvey and other recent disasters.

About 20 members of the First United Methodist Church had gathered for a holiday meal. Afterward, the group discussed firearms and how they should be handled in a church setting. The discussion reportedly followed similar gun-safety seminars held by a nearby sheriff’s department.

Tellico Plains Police Chief Russ Parks said the man showed the group a .38-caliber Ruger handgun he was carrying. He removed the magazine and cleared the chamber while demonstrating the firearm, according to authorities.

Later, as members of the group were cleaning up, another parishioner who had not seen the demonstration asked to look at the gun. The man handled the firearm, which still had a round in the chamber, and it discharged.

The bullet passed through the man’s hand before striking his 80-year-old wife, who was seated in a wheelchair beside him. Authorities said the bullet entered her lower abdomen, exited on the opposite side, and then struck her forearm before ricocheting off a wall and coming to rest beneath the wheelchair.

The shooting caused confusion inside the church, with some people initially believing that an armed attacker might be present. Church members called 911, and emergency responders took the injured couple to a hospital.

Both were flown to the University of Tennessee Medical Center for treatment. Authorities initially described their conditions as critical. Police said the shooting appeared to be accidental and did not report evidence of an active assailant.

The incident underscored the importance of treating every firearm as loaded and following basic safety procedures, including keeping the gun pointed in a safe direction and keeping one’s finger away from the trigger.

During Roy Moore’s 2017 campaign for the U.S. Senate, several women accused the Alabama Republican of pursuing or sexually harassing them when they were teenagers. Moore denied the allegations.

A separate account concerned Moore’s alleged presence at the Gadsden Mall, where he reportedly encountered young women while working as an assistant district attorney. Becky Gray, who said she worked at the mall and was in her early 20s at the time, described Moore’s repeated visits to her department.

Gray said Moore would stop to talk with her when he came through the store and that his attention eventually made her uncomfortable.

“I went to my manager and talked to him about it and asked him, basically, what could be done,” Gray said in an account reported by ABC News. She said a manager later told her that Moore had been banned from the mall.

Gray also recalled Moore spending time at the mall on Friday and Saturday nights, when many younger people gathered there. “It just kind of got creepy to me,” she said.

Another former mall employee, identified in reports as Greg Legat, also said Moore had been barred from the property. His account was presented as supporting Gray’s recollection, although the circumstances and timing of any ban were not independently established in the reports.

The mall allegations were separate from the accusations by women who said Moore pursued them or had sexual contact with them when they were teenagers. Those women’s accounts became a central issue in Moore’s Senate campaign, which he ultimately lost to Democrat Doug Jones.

Gray’s account does not by itself establish that Moore sexually harassed or assaulted anyone, and reports about the alleged mall ban did not provide definitive documentation from the mall. Moore rejected the broader allegations against him and questioned the accounts made public during the campaign.

The claims about Moore’s conduct remained part of the controversy surrounding his candidacy and prompted renewed scrutiny of his interactions with young women before he entered statewide politics.

Trump Administration Moves to Allow Some African Elephant Trophy Imports

The Trump administration announced in November 2017 that it would begin allowing the import of certain sport-hunted elephant trophies from Zimbabwe into the United States, reversing a suspension imposed during the Obama administration. The decision concerned permits issued under the Endangered Species Act and did not repeal the law or create a blanket authorization for elephant trophies.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service said it had determined that importing legally hunted elephants from Zimbabwe could benefit conservation under specific conditions. The agency said revenues from regulated hunting may support local communities and wildlife-management programs, although conservation groups questioned whether the policy would provide meaningful protection for elephants.

The announcement drew attention in part because Donald Trump Jr. has previously hunted an elephant in Zimbabwe and posted photographs from the trip. His brother, Eric Trump, has also participated in big-game hunting. The president’s sons were not identified as applicants for permits under the new policy.

African elephants are protected under the Endangered Species Act, but the law allows the government to authorize imports when it concludes that hunting is legal, properly managed and contributes to the survival of the species. Each application must be evaluated separately, and the decision does not authorize the importation of illegally obtained trophies.

The policy was announced amid continuing concern over the decline of African elephant populations. The 2016 Great Elephant Census estimated that savanna elephant numbers fell by about 30 percent between 2007 and 2014, largely because of poaching and habitat loss. The United States and other countries have taken steps to restrict the ivory trade, while some African countries have argued that tightly regulated hunting and limited ivory sales could generate funding for conservation. Texas Sheriff Draws Criticism After Raising Possible Disorderly Conduct Charge Over Anti-Trump Sticker

Fort Bend County Sheriff Troy E. Nehls drew criticism after posting on Facebook about an anti-Trump sticker displayed on a truck frequently seen along FM 359.

“I have received numerous calls regarding the offensive display on this truck,” Nehls wrote. He asked anyone who knew the owner—or owned the truck—to contact him so they could discuss the matter.

The sheriff also said the county prosecutor had indicated that a disorderly conduct charge could be considered, although he suggested that the issue might instead be resolved through an agreement to modify the sticker. The post did not indicate that anyone had been charged or arrested.

The incident prompted questions about whether the sticker constituted protected political expression. Criticism of the president or other public officials is generally protected by the First Amendment, although speech can be subject to narrow restrictions in circumstances not involving the expression of a political opinion.

The Supreme Court addressed related issues in its 1971 decision in *Cohen v. California*. In that case, the court overturned the conviction of a man who had worn a jacket bearing an expletive directed at the military draft, ruling that the government could not punish him merely for displaying the message in public.

The case involving the truck remained a matter of public discussion after the sheriff’s post. The available account did not establish that prosecutors filed charges or that the truck’s owner agreed to change the sticker.

On Tuesday, Donald Trump told reporters a story about Air Force One and former President Barack Obama that appears to be incorrect. Before boarding the plane to return home from the Philippines, Trump said Air Force One had once been denied landing rights there during a trip by his predecessor because relations between the United States and the Philippines were poor.

Trump said Air Force One “never got to land” in the Philippines while describing his own relationship with the Southeast Asian nation as “very strong.”

“And as you know, we were having a lot of problems with the Philippines. The relationship with the past administration was horrible, to use a nice word,” Trump told reporters in Manila. “I would say ‘horrible’ is putting it mildly. You know what happened. Many of you were there, and you never got to land,” he continued. “The plane came close but it didn’t land.”

In September 2016, Obama called off a planned meeting with Duterte in Laos after Duterte directed an obscene remark at him. Duterte had objected to questions about his government’s violent campaign against illegal drugs.

Obama also visited the Philippines earlier in his presidency and signed an enhanced defense cooperation agreement with the country in 2014. Trump said that the relationship between the United States and the Philippines was “probably better than ever before.”

“So it’s very important that we get along with the Philippines, and we really do. We have a very good relationship,” he said. “I would actually say probably better than ever before.”

Duterte’s campaign against suspected drug dealers and users has drawn condemnation from human rights organizations and the United Nations. The number of deaths has been disputed, with Philippine authorities reporting thousands of fatalities and rights groups alleging that the toll was substantially higher. Duterte has defended the campaign and made repeated remarks supporting lethal force.

During Trump’s visit, human rights groups criticized him for not publicly pressing Duterte over the killings. The White House said the two leaders discussed issues including terrorism, trade and regional security. Trump’s account of Obama’s arrival in the Philippines, however, is inconsistent with records of the 2015 visit.

OOPS: Trump Judicial Nominee Faced Questions Over Failure To Disclose Marriage To White House Attorney

When the Senate Judiciary Committee approved along party lines Donald Trump’s nomination of Brett Talley to a federal judgeship in Alabama, questions emerged about information omitted from his disclosure materials. Talley is married to Ann Donaldson, who served as chief of staff to White House counsel Donald McGahn.

According to reporting by The New York Times, Talley was asked in his publicly released Senate questionnaire to identify family members and others who could present potential conflicts of interest. He did not list his wife.

The omission drew scrutiny because federal district judges can issue rulings involving the executive branch and its lawyers. During the confirmation process, Talley also described frequent contact with White House lawyers but did not identify Donaldson as his spouse in the questionnaire.

Talley’s professional qualifications also became a central issue in the nomination. He had not tried a case, and the American Bar Association rated him “not qualified” for the position in a unanimous assessment, an unusual finding for a judicial nominee.

The Senate Judiciary Committee advanced Talley’s nomination, but the full Senate did not confirm him. His nomination was later returned to the White House and was not ultimately approved.

The disclosure issue and the ABA’s assessment prompted criticism from Democrats and legal observers, who questioned whether Talley had sufficient courtroom experience and whether his personal and professional connections had been fully presented to senators. Supporters of the nomination argued that the Senate should evaluate his qualifications through the confirmation process.

The episode highlighted the scrutiny applied to judicial nominees’ experience, ethics disclosures and potential conflicts of interest. It also raised questions about how the Senate reviews nominees whose professional relationships include senior administration officials.

Trump Chuckles After Philippine Leader Calls Journalists “Spies” During ASEAN Summit

U.S. President Donald Trump and Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte exchanged friendly remarks during a bilateral meeting in Manila on Monday, despite international criticism of Duterte’s human-rights record.

Trump chuckled after Duterte referred to journalists as “spies” while reporters were being asked to leave the room. The exchange occurred as members of the press tried to ask about human rights.

“We will be talking on matters that are of interest to both the Philippines and the United States,” Duterte said, according to accounts from reporters present. “With you around, guys, you are the spies.”

Bloomberg reporter Jennifer Jacobs described the exchange in a post on social media. She wrote that Duterte made the remark as the press was being ushered out of the meeting, and that Trump chuckled.

When reporters asked Trump whether he would raise human rights with Duterte, the Philippine leader interrupted and said the gathering was not a news conference. Duterte later told reporters, “I would like for the media to leave us alone,” before they exited the room.

The meeting took place as Duterte faced international scrutiny over his administration’s campaign against illegal drugs. Philippine authorities have reported thousands of deaths in police operations, while human-rights groups have alleged that the number of victims is substantially higher and have called for independent investigations.

Duterte has repeatedly dismissed criticism of the campaign and has used hostile language toward journalists and political opponents. His relationship with the United States had deteriorated during President Barack Obama’s administration, after Obama expressed concern about human rights in the Philippines. Duterte responded with an insult directed at Obama and pursued closer relations with China and Russia.

Trump, by contrast, had adopted a warmer tone toward Duterte. During their meeting, the two leaders discussed bilateral relations and regional issues, but there was no public indication that Trump directly challenged Duterte over the drug war or other allegations of abuses. Trump had also invited Duterte to visit the White House, an invitation that drew criticism from human-rights advocates.

The treatment of journalists at the Manila meeting attracted additional attention because the Philippines has long been considered a dangerous country for members of the press. International press-freedom organizations have documented numerous journalist killings there over several decades, particularly in connection with political and local government disputes. Impunity in many of those cases has remained a longstanding concern.

Trump had frequently criticized news organizations during his presidential campaign and continued to accuse some journalists of publishing “fake news” after taking office. Duterte has likewise attacked critical media outlets and reporters.

The brief exchange in Manila therefore prompted criticism from press-freedom advocates, who said the leaders’ lighthearted response contrasted with the seriousness of threats facing journalists in the Philippines. The White House did not publicly announce any new human-rights commitments arising from the meeting.
